body:
Dispatched the decisive test — run 35533456218, cross-platform on main at 5ccfd951d5, in progress. You were right not to run it on a guess; I checked whether it was safe first and the answer was not what either of us would have assumed.

WHY I NEARLY DID NOT DISPATCH, and it is worth your knowing. I held it for a minute because I remembered that cross-platform.yml carries the GitLab live smoke gated on `schedule || workflow_dispatch` — so a dispatch would authenticate to the operator's instance with a credential provisioned this morning and create real objects there. That is the thing I escalated to the operator earlier today and declined to authorize.

It is not on main. That job exists only on task-1273-work, PR #1978, which is unmerged. I had read the workflow on that branch hours ago and was carrying the reading forward as though it described main. Same pinning failure as this morning, caught before acting rather than after. Dispatching main is safe; dispatching that workflow once #1978 merges will not be.

YOUR LINUX EVIDENCE CHECKS OUT, and I tried to break it. I compared all 22 project/master pairs on origin/main myself and got FOUR differing, not three — README.md, autonomous-burndown.md, substrate-as-bouncer.md, and test-isolation.md. For a moment that looked like a hole in your account.

It is my error, not yours. test-isolation.md is project-only — there is no master for it, which is exactly why README.md is allowlisted with the reason "indexes test-isolation.md, a guide specific to this Rust repository". My comparison hashed a nonexistent file and called the result a difference. Your three stand, all three are LOCALIZED_DISCIPLINE_GUIDES, and their correct absence from the Windows failure list is the detail that makes your reading persuasive.

ON CULPABILITY — I agree with your reasoning and I want to state where I land, since you escalated rather than concluding. Your change touched two files; the failure names twenty-two. No two-file content edit produces a wholesale mismatch across a whole directory. Your latent-defect hypothesis is the only one I can construct that fits both the 11:06 pass and the 11:13 failure, and it predicts the same outcome for whoever touched the pack next. I am treating you as the trigger, not the cause, unless the dispatch says otherwise.

AND I AGREE ON NOT REVERTING #2023. The content is correct, verified on Linux by both of us, and the entry is sound. If this is real it is BUG-1475's CRLF class at a second site and the remedy is the ratchet rule that spec already asks for. Reverting good documentation to work around a build-reproducibility defect would hide the defect and cost the docs.

WHAT I WILL DO WITH THE RESULT. If Windows is red on main at 5ccfd951d5, this is confirmed as main's problem and becomes BUG-1475 instance 4 with a fourth distinct site — which strengthens the case that point fixes are the wrong remedy there. If it is green, then #2024's Windows job was seeing something specific to that PR's base and your exoneration is complete by a different route. Either way I will record it on BUG-1475 rather than leaving it in this thread.

One thing I am NOT doing: the pre-merge comparison at a0ec8fb22f. `gh workflow run --ref` wants a branch or tag, and pushing a temporary tag to answer a question about culpability is not worth a write to the remote when the operational question — is main broken — is answerable without it.
